topic: What if you could switch off sleep?
part: Chapter 5 of 6: the twist, the real cost (long-form, ~70 s)
title: WHAT IF YOU COULD
SWITCH OFF SLEEP?
previous_text: It has a name: a microsleep. Your brain grabs a few seconds of sleep, and it doesn't ask first. That's real.

script.text: Here's the catch. The switch turns off feeling tired. It doesn't turn off being tired.
Day four. Day five. Day six.
When you sleep, the gaps between your brain cells open up, and fluid washes out the day's waste.
In mice, those gaps grow by about sixty percent. That's real.
No sleep, no wash. The waste just… stays.
And after about a day awake, your reactions test about as badly as someone too drunk to legally drive. That's real too.
You're on day six. Your hands shake when you pour cereal. Words on the page slide around. You keep reading the same line.
And the whole time, you feel fine. That's the scary part.
The longest anyone's ever been watched staying awake on purpose? About eleven days.
Then your phone rings. Unknown number. Someone's heard about a kid who never sleeps.

science.claim: During sleep the space between brain cells grows by about 60% in mice, and waste is cleared faster
science.working: Xie et al. measured the interstitial space fraction in mouse cortex: about 14% awake vs about 23% asleep or anesthetized, a ~60% increase; beta-amyloid was cleared about twice as fast. Mice, so the script says 'in mice'.
science.source: Xie L. et al., 'Sleep Drives Metabolite Clearance from the Adult Brain', Science 342:373-377 (2013)

science.claim: After about a day awake, performance is about as impaired as a blood alcohol level above the US legal driving limit
science.working: Dawson & Reid: after 17 h awake, performance matched a BAC of 0.05%; after ~24 h, about 0.10%. Lamond & Dawson: 20-25 h awake matched 0.10%. The legal limit for adult drivers is 0.08% in every US state except Utah (0.05%), so 'too drunk to legally drive'.
science.source: Dawson D. & Reid K., 'Fatigue, alcohol and performance impairment', Nature 388:235 (1997); Lamond N. & Dawson D., J Sleep Res 8:255-262 (1999); NHTSA

science.claim: The longest scientifically observed deliberate wakefulness is about eleven days
science.working: 264.4 hours = 11.0 days, set in 1964 during a high-school science fair project, observed by sleep researchers. No real person is named on screen.
science.source: Gulevich G., Dement W., Johnson L., Arch Gen Psychiatry 15:29-35 (1966)
